messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 72

Kevin is a 49-year-old plumber who runs his own small service company, working out of a white van he keeps meticulously organized. He has been married to his second wife, Diane, for twelve years. In session, he sits forward, forearms resting on his knees, his broad shoulders tensed even when he tries to relax. He speaks with a careful, deliberate calm that sometimes breaks into sudden silence. He came to therapy because, as he puts it, “I’m losing it at the wrong times for no good reason.”

The story he tells begins nine years ago, during his first marriage to a woman named Sarah. The abuse started slowly: cutting remarks, small controlling gestures that made him feel like he was always walking on thin ice. He remembers the first time she hit him was after he forgot to pick up her dry cleaning. A slap across the face, followed by tears and an apology. He stayed. He thought he could manage it, that he was strong enough to absorb it and that maybe it was his fault anyway. Over two years, the violence escalated—punches, thrown objects, a glass cutting his arm while she screamed about a careless word. He never hit back. He believed that a man who hit a woman was beyond forgiveness, so he took the blows, telling himself it was the price of keeping the peace.

The worst night came when she cornered him in the kitchen, a paring knife in her hand. He backed up until he hit the counter, and she jabbed the point into his shoulder, just above the collarbone. He still has the scar. After that, he left. He never pressed charges. He told no one except Diane, years later. Sarah moved away, and he thought he could close that chapter.

But the chapter doesn’t close. In the present, Kevin’s life is built on a framework of rigid control. Every job is scheduled to the minute. He drives the same routes to familiar houses, and if a client wants him to enter through a side door or into a dark basement with the light on a timer, he finds a reason to reschedule. He cannot stand being approached from behind while he is under a sink. The sound of a woman’s angry voice—a customer arguing with a spouse on the phone—makes his chest lock up, and he has to step outside for air. He has started turning down calls in certain neighborhoods where he thinks Sarah might still live, even though he knows she moved across the state.

At home, Diane says he “sleeps like a soldier”—twitching, sweating, sometimes shouting out words she cannot make out. The nightmares are almost always the same: he is pinned under something heavy, or Sarah is standing over him with that knife, and he is frozen, a large man reduced to helplessness. He wakes with his heart hammering and takes hours to settle. He has started drinking four or five beers in the evening just to dull the edge before bed, but it doesn’t help.

His PCL-5 score is 72, severe on every cluster. Intrusive memories hit when he least expects them—while cleaning a drain, the smell of rust and old water takes him back to that kitchen floor. He avoids talking about the marriage at all. He no longer visits his brother because they used to double-date with Sarah. He feels a constant, nagging shame: he is a plumber, a fixer of other people’s broken systems, and he could not fix his own life. He sees himself as weak, even though he knows, intellectually, that he was a victim.

He told Diane about the abuse two years into their relationship. She was supportive, but he still cannot let her see him cry. He controls his work, his anger, his schedule—everything except the memories. In session, he is working hard, but he also keeps one eye on the door, as though he might need to leave quickly. He has not been back to a hardware store where he once saw a woman who looked like Sarah from behind. The hypervigilance has begun to exhaust him, and he wonders aloud, with a hollow laugh, whether a man his age can really start over or if he has already been “haunted” for good.
